title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion
authors: Li Zheng, Simin Chen
abstract: Finite element method (FEM) solvers are foundational to scientific and engineering simulation, yet their susceptibility to \emph{efficiency attacks} remains largely unexplored. An adversary can craft syntactically valid and runnable FEM programs that complete successfully while forcing excessive computational work, enabling computational denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Finding such inputs is challenging because FEM programs occupy a vast, structured space constrained by numerical, geometric, and constitutive requirements. We introduce CloakFEM, a domain-guided LLM-agent framework for automatically generating runnable adversarial FEM programs that amplify solver computation. CloakFEM combines LLM-guided search with an FEM-specific intermediate representation and a deterministic validity gate that enforces runnable constraints. Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM discovers adversarial inputs that substantially amplify solver work while remaining valid and solvable. In the most extreme case, solver iterations increase from 43 to 247,367, a \(5{,}752.72\times\) amplification. CloakFEM outperforms five generic black-box baselines and retains an advantage over evolutionary search under a controlled bounded action space. Cross-solver analysis further reveals both problem-intrinsic and solver-specific sources of vulnerability. Our results uncover an underexplored efficiency-attack surface in FEM solvers and show that runnable FEM programs can serve as adversarial inputs.

infographic.key_insight: CloakFEM shows that valid, solvable FEM programs can act as efficiency attacks, increasing solver iterations by up to 5,752.72×.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Simulation services may face computational denial-of-service risks even when submitted FEM models run successfully.
method: Use an LLM agent to search for FEM programs that amplify solver computation.
Represent candidates with an FEM-specific intermediate representation.
Apply a deterministic validity gate to enforce runnable constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM outperformed five generic black-box baselines; the extreme case increased iterations from 43 to 247,367.
infographic.watch_item: The reported peak amplification concerns iteration count, not necessarily equivalent wall-clock slowdown, and vulnerabilities vary by problem and solver.
infographic.paper_title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion

title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 3D
authors: Tommaso Bevilacqua, Axel Klawonn, Martin Lanser, Adam Wasiak
abstract: Overlapping Schwarz methods are among the most successful domain decomposition preconditioners for large-scale finite element simulations. In this work, the Generalized Dryja-Smith-Widlund (GDSW), GDSW$^*$, and Reduced GDSW (RGDSW) coarse spaces are studied for three-dimensional high-order finite element method (FEM) and virtual element method (VEM) for the Poisson equation and the equations of linear elasticity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of GDSW-type coarse spaces for polynomial degrees $k\ge 3$ in three dimensions, for either discretization. In 3D VEM, the face degrees of freedom (DOFs) are moments instead of point values. The kernel of the differential operator, which defines the interface values of the GDSW coarse basis functions, must be represented through these moments. The construction is therefore no longer purely algebraic and, without this correction, the coarse level loses its effect for $k\ge 3$. FEM and VEM are tested on hexahedral meshes, and VEM is additionally tested on polyhedral ones. Polynomial degrees up to $k=5$ and runs on up to $4\,096$ subdomains and parallel cores are included in the numerical study. Numerical experiments show scalable iteration counts for all coarse space variants for the Poisson problem, illustrating the expected trade-off between the coarse space size and robustness. Further experiments for linear elasticity confirms that the moment-based construction extends naturally from the scalar to the vector-valued problem.

infographic.key_insight: GDSW-type coarse spaces support scalable high-order 3D domain decomposition, but VEM requires moment-based kernel representation to retain coarse-level effectiveness for polynomial degrees k ≥ 3.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These preconditioners support efficient parallel finite element and virtual element simulations, including 3D linear elasticity.
method: Use two-level overlapping additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW, GDSW*, or reduced GDSW coarse spaces.
Represent operator kernels through face moments when constructing VEM coarse basis functions.
Evaluate high-order FEM and VEM for Poisson and linear elasticity problems.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests reached polynomial degree k = 5 and 4,096 subdomains and parallel cores, showing scalable Poisson iteration counts across all coarse-space variants and extension of the moment-based construction to elasticity.
infographic.watch_item: VEM coarse-space construction is not purely algebraic: omitting the face-moment correction makes the coarse level ineffective for k ≥ 3.
infographic.paper_title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 3D

title: Derivation of Novel Isotropic Metamaterials at the Hashin Shtrikman Stiffness Limit Enabled by Physics Informed Neural Networks
authors: Manish Kumar Singh, Dominic Kang Jueh Lim, Anson Wen Han Cheong, Adams Wai Kin Kong, Chang Quan Lai
abstract: Current methods of deriving ultrastiff isotropic metamaterials require heuristics or topology optimization, which are highly inefficient and limited by human input. To circumvent this, Physics Informed Neural Networks are applied to analytical equations to systematically solve for plate orientations in closed cell lattices. Following a standardized procedure, the plate orientations were modelled and assembled into geometries resembling quasi random foams for validation via finite element simulations. Closed cell 6-plate geometries were also additively manufactured using LAPIS and experimentally characterized. The results indicate that a minimum of 6 plates is required to constitute an ultrastiff isotropic lattice, 7 plates would return the established plate Cubic Octet structure while 8 to 10 plate geometries did not show significant differences in properties. Despite the introduction of some plate bending due to sub-optimal plate placement strategy, relative stiffness of the PINNs lattices adheres closely to the Hashin Shtrikman upper bound, 90 percent of Hashin Shtrikman upper bound at a relative density of 0.4, and the lattices maintain near isotropic behaviour, achieving a Zener ratio of 0.95 at a relative density of 0.1. Benchmarking results show that specific stiffness of PINNs lattices is higher than the majority of isotropic architectures reported in the literature.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-informed neural networks identify plate orientations for near-isotropic, ultrastiff closed-cell lattices, with at least six plates required.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These architectures offer a route to lightweight structures with high stiffness and nearly direction-independent mechanical response.
method: Use PINNs to solve analytical equations for plate orientations.
Assemble orientations into foam-like closed-cell geometries and validate with finite element simulations.
Additively manufacture six-plate lattices using LAPIS and characterize experimentally.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported lattices reach 90% of the Hashin–Shtrikman stiffness upper bound at relative density 0.4 and a near-isotropic Zener ratio of 0.95 at relative density 0.1.
infographic.watch_item: Suboptimal plate placement introduces bending, so orientation solutions alone do not ensure ideal stiffness in assembled lattices.
infographic.paper_title: Derivation of Novel Isotropic Metamaterials at the Hashin Shtrikman Stiffness Limit Enabled by Physics Informed Neural Networks

title: Remap for ALE Hydrodynamics via Direct Interpolation and Constraint Optimization
authors: Brendan Keith, Dohyun Kim, Boyan Lazarov, Ketan Mittal, Cosmin G. Petra, Mathias R. Schmidt
abstract: This work presents an optimization-based remap approach for arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) hydrodynamics that preserves sharp features and physical bounds while conserving global quantities such as volume, mass, momentum, and total energy. Achieving these properties is the main challenge in remap methods. The presented approach is well-suited for high-order finite element (FE) discretizations and ALE methods that allow for large, purely Lagrangian displacements between successive remeshing and remapping steps. Recent advances in parallel, GPU-capable interpolation routines enable the initial transfer of all fields via direct physical-space interpolation, avoiding computationally costly and diffusive pseudo-transient PDE-based advection. The interpolation produces bounded fields with minimal numerical diffusion. However, it may violate the desired conservation of global properties. Thus, a subsequent optimization step restores conservation while preserving physical bounds. The presented method provides minimally diffusive remapping of finite element fields of arbitrary order. Moreover, it directly remaps quantities defined at integration points, eliminating the need for projection onto finite element spaces. The approach also mitigates typical challenges associated with synchronizing primal variables and conserved quantities in advection-based remap methods. The proposed optimization-based remap method is evaluated using standard two- and three-dimensional remap benchmarks and full ALE hydrodynamics simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Direct interpolation followed by constraint optimization enables minimally diffusive ALE remapping while preserving physical bounds and restoring global conservation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports high-order hydrodynamics simulations with large mesh displacements while conserving volume, mass, momentum, and total energy.
method: Transfer fields by direct physical-space interpolation using parallel, GPU-capable routines.
Apply constraint optimization to restore global conservation while retaining physical bounds.
Remap arbitrary-order finite element fields and integration-point quantities without intermediate projection.
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach is evaluated on standard 2D and 3D remap benchmarks and full ALE hydrodynamics simulations; the abstract provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: The cost and scalability of the conservation-restoring optimization require assessment for large production simulations.
infographic.paper_title: Remap for ALE Hydrodynamics via Direct Interpolation and Constraint Optimization

title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
authors: Suhas Suresh Bharadwaj
abstract: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.

infographic.key_insight: On simulated wavefields, a PINN with exact boundary and initial constraints accurately identifies the shear piezoelectric coefficient e15 without boundary or initial-condition penalty tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a potential non-destructive alternative to dedicated resonance tests for characterizing shear coupling in PMUTs and surface acoustic wave devices.
method: Embed spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers to enforce clamped, grounded boundaries and a resting initial state exactly.
Train on coupled electro-elastodynamic equations and sparse, noisy wavefield observations.
Non-dimensionalize governing coefficients to comparable scales near unity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The full formulation achieved 1.19% mean e15 error on finite-element data at 30 dB noise and 0.65–2.71% across a 40–0 dB sweep; displacement-only training achieved 0.45% mean error on finite-element data.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is simulation-only; experimental performance and constructing exact constraint functions for complex device geometries remain untested.
infographic.paper_title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints

title: Process-zone condensation: a discretization-exact reduced cell model for FE$^2$ analysis of composites with fibre-matrix debonding and matrix plasticity
authors: Leonilson Toffoli Pedrini, Maycoln Conci, Rafael Marin Ferro
abstract: Periodic composites with cohesive interfaces and matrix plasticity require nonlinear cell solutions in multiscale analysis. Process-zone condensation eliminates the linear elastic remainder of the cell by a Schur complement, retaining all interfacial and process-zone internal variables. Influence matrices recover macroscopic stress and consistent tangent. One back-substitution per increment checks that the matrix outside the retained zone remains elastic. While this holds, the reduction is exact relative to the full discretisation, also with a plastic matrix, and requires no training. In an E-glass/epoxy cell, eight of nine two-dimensional paths agree with the full cell to 1e-11 in stress and tangent; the check flags the ninth. Three paths on each of two three-dimensional meshes need zone expansion. Excluding setup and checks, two-dimensional path timings show an aggregate speed-up of 3.3; certified three-dimensional zones show none. In adaptive finite element squared (FE$^2$) simulations of a perforated plate, the reduced solver reproduces the full-cell response within solver tolerances, 1.51 times faster for glass/polypropylene and slower for glass/epoxy. Independent Ansys models agree to below 1e-3 in cell stress and about 0.6% in plate reactions, although local damage and plasticity onsets differ. The advantage depends on zone size, active set and adaptation costs.

infographic.key_insight: Process-zone condensation is exact relative to the full cell discretisation while the eliminated matrix region remains elastic, retaining cohesive interfaces and process-zone plasticity without training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method can accelerate FE² analysis of composite debonding and matrix plasticity without sacrificing full-cell accuracy, but speed gains depend on the material and retained-zone size.
method: Eliminate the linear-elastic cell remainder using a Schur complement.
Recover macroscopic stress and consistent tangent through influence matrices.
Check the eliminated region once per increment by back-substitution and expand the retained zone when needed.
infographic.evidence_signal: Eight of nine 2D paths matched full-cell stress and tangent to 1e-11, with the ninth flagged; aggregate 2D speed-up was 3.3× excluding setup and checks, while plate-level FE² was 1.51× faster for glass/polypropylene but slower for glass/epoxy.
infographic.watch_item: Exactness requires the eliminated region to remain elastic; zone expansion, active-set changes and adaptation costs can erase computational savings, as observed in certified 3D cases.
infographic.paper_title: Process-zone condensation: a discretization-exact reduced cell model for FE$^2$ analysis of composites with fibre-matrix debonding and matrix plasticity

title: ENGINE: Endogenous Variational MultiScale Optimization for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning
authors: Zhuoli Ouyang, Changxi Chi, Siyuan Li, Tailin Wu
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient large language model (LLM) fine-tuning, and recent methods incorporate curvature-aware strategies. However, in the high-dimensional parameter space of LLMs, these methods inherently suffer from exploding gradient variance and prohibitive costs. Conversely, confining updates to a low-dimensional subspace reduces variance but discards critical high-dimensional information, degrading performance. This creates a fundamental dilemma: full-space optimization is informative but has high variance, while subspace optimization has low variance but loses information. To break this trade-off, we propose ENGINE (Endogenous Variational MultiScale). Inspired by computational mechanics, we adapt static Variational MultiScale (VMS) theory to dynamic optimization, treating low- and high-dimensional spaces as resolved coarse and unresolved fine scales. Through a multigrid-style V-cycle, ENGINE alternates between spaces, dynamically probing fine-grained information in the high-dimensional space and injecting it to correct the efficient low-dimensional sampling process. Under appropriate assumptions, statistical analysis characterizes variance reduction and correction of curvature-induced bias, and convergence analysis establishes a stationarity bound for the corrected coarse updates. Evaluations on standard LLM benchmarks show that ENGINE achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence than existing ZO methods, achieving up to a $2.61\times$ speed-up in forward passes with zero additional peak memory overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/ENGINE.

infographic.key_insight: ENGINE bridges the variance–information trade-off in zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning by using high-dimensional probes to correct low-dimensional updates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It adapts variational multiscale ideas from computational mechanics to improve memory-efficient LLM optimization.
method: Treat low- and high-dimensional parameter spaces as coarse and fine scales.
Alternate between scales through a multigrid-style V-cycle.
Inject fine-scale information to correct coarse-scale sampling.
infographic.evidence_signal: On standard LLM benchmarks, ENGINE reports higher accuracy and faster convergence than existing zeroth-order methods, with up to 2.61× speed-up in forward passes and no additional peak memory overhead.
infographic.watch_item: Theoretical guarantees depend on assumptions, and the abstract does not specify how gains vary across models, tasks, or probing schedules.
infographic.paper_title: ENGINE: Endogenous Variational MultiScale Optimization for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning

title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning
authors: Tom Saliencro, Wen-Hsuan Liu, Rohan Desai, Amara Okonkwo, Maya Lindqvist
abstract: Exemplar-free continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers increasingly relies on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), yet prevailing methods govern the low-rank update space through strict subspace isolation. By projecting each incoming task into the approximate null space of historical token activations, isolation-based learners equate any cross-task feature overlap with catastrophic interference. We show that this orthogonality premise induces a structural bottleneck we term \emph{spectral starvation}: when down-projection bases are locked before task optimization, the gradient norm reaching the trainable up-projection is upper-bounded by the energy of current-task features captured by the chosen basis. Because natural visual tasks share low- and mid-level covariance structure, historical null tails contain barely $5.5\%$ of incoming task variance, starving new-class plasticity while blocking positive consolidation along shared directions. We propose BISECT (Bilevel Spectral Decomposition), a continual LoRA framework that partitions a fixed rank-$r$ budget into two orthogonal functional blocks: an invariant carrier spanned by the dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix, and a novelty complement extracted via generalized Rayleigh whitening followed by orthogonal complement projection. After single-task training, BISECT folds both blocks back into the frozen backbone using a closed-form precision gate that scales each rank-1 invariant atom by its current-to-joint Rayleigh ratio while preserving novelty atoms at unit gain. Across eight incremental settings on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and DomainNet, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines with zero extra inference parameters or FLOPs, and remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.

infographic.key_insight: BISECT addresses spectral starvation in continual LoRA learning by splitting a fixed low-rank budget into shared invariant directions and complementary novelty directions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Although categorized as constitutive modeling, this work evaluates continual visual learning, so its relevance to mechanics is methodological rather than demonstrated.
method: Build an invariant carrier from dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix.
Extract an orthogonal novelty complement using generalized Rayleigh whitening and complement projection.
Fold trained updates into the backbone, gating invariant atoms by current-to-joint Rayleigh ratios and retaining novelty atoms at unit gain.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that historical null tails capture only 5.5% of incoming-task variance and that BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines across eight incremental settings on five vision datasets, with no extra inference parameters or FLOPs.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify training-time spectral decomposition costs or validate performance on constitutive-modeling tasks.
infographic.paper_title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning

title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA
authors: Wen-Hsuan Liu, Amara Okonkwo, Tom Saliencro, Rohan Desai, Maya Lindqvist
abstract: Parameter-efficient continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers largely relies on a costly premise: preventing catastrophic forgetting requires either spawning a dedicated LoRA branch per session---causing adapter parameters to scale linearly with task horizon---or applying sparse Mixture-of-Experts gating symmetrically to both forward and backward passes, which sacrifices representational rank at test time. We argue that reading consolidated knowledge and writing new task credit are fundamentally asymmetric operations. Because visual features in a shared low-rank space distribute across rank-1 atoms rather than localizing in disjoint task silos, forward inference should read all atoms at full rank capacity, whereas backward optimization should restrict plasticity to a sparse subset of input-aligned channels. We introduce RASP (Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity LoRA), which adapts a single stationary-size adapter across sequential tasks. At each step, a scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-$q$ unlocked atoms to receive gradients, blocks updates on the remaining $r-q$ channels, and penalizes Frobenius Gram coherence between active and non-updated output directions. Across sessions, the router's empirical activation trace and each atom's exact spectral norm form a zero-overhead geometric consolidation index $ω_j = \sqrt{\tilde{c}_j \tildeσ_j}$ that drives Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking. Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, RASP matches or surpasses branch-expanding LoRA learners under a strictly constant parameter footprint.

infographic.key_insight: RASP separates reading from learning: inference uses every LoRA atom, while training updates only a sparse subset within one fixed-size adapter.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support memory-constrained continual adaptation of engineering vision systems, but the abstract does not demonstrate constitutive modeling or solid-mechanics applications.
method: A scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-q unlocked atoms for gradient updates while retaining all atoms for inference.
A Gram-coherence penalty discourages overlap between active and non-updated output directions.
Activation traces and atom spectral norms guide Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking to consolidate knowledge.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, the abstract reports matching or surpassing branch-expanding LoRA learners with a constant adapter parameter footprint.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical results or routing-cost measurements, so accuracy gains and runtime overhead require verification.
infographic.paper_title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA

title: Manifold Embedding of Deep Image Features for Image Matching via Neural Adjoint Maps
authors: Nafie El Amrani, Moritz Heep, Florian Bernard
abstract: Estimating semantic correspondences between different object instances of similar categories in real-world images is a fundamental challenge in computer vision. While the recent progress in foundation models has significantly advanced solutions for such difficult image correspondence problems, respective methods are often insufficiently regularised. For example, common nearest-neighbour matching with foundation model features often results in noisy correspondences, which is particularly prominent when solving for dense correspondences. In this work, we tackle image matching via functional maps, which have been popularised for 3D shape matching due to their powerful spectral formalism utilising an efficient low-dimensional linear representation. However, functional maps require that domains (in our cases the rectangular image grids) are equipped with an informative and non-trivial geometry. To define a meaningful manifold structure for images, we use Galerkin's method from finite elements to derive a discrete Laplace-Beltrami operator (LBO) based on a manifold embedding of deep image features. Further, we leverage a neural adjoint map that allows to represent non-linear mappings. We demonstrate that our method sets the new state of the art among zero-shot image correspondence methods on multiple dense correspondence benchmarks of real-world images. Our code is publicly available: https://github.com/NafieAmrani/NAMI

infographic.key_insight: Embedding deep image features as a manifold enables geometry-aware functional maps that regularise dense semantic image matching.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work transfers finite-element Galerkin discretisation to computer vision rather than providing a solid-mechanics or FEM surrogate model.
method: Construct an image manifold from deep feature embeddings.
Derive a discrete Laplace–Beltrami operator using finite-element Galerkin methods.
Combine spectral functional maps with a neural adjoint map to represent nonlinear correspondences.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on multiple real-world dense correspondence benchmarks, without naming datasets or giving numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify computational cost or sensitivity to the choice of deep features and manifold construction.
infographic.paper_title: Manifold Embedding of Deep Image Features for Image Matching via Neural Adjoint Maps

title: Coupled Soft-Clamped Polygon Resonators with Tunable Mechanical Coupling
authors: Zhihao Niu, Peng Chen, Shenggen Zheng, Yuan-Yuan Zhao, Yuanyuan Zhao
abstract: Coupler geometry controls both the frequency splitting and the dissipation of coupled polygon resonators. We develop a continuum model for two identical square-shaped resonators coupled by a shared tether and compare the analytical predictions with finite element simulations. The model relates the coupler length and width to the frequency splitting and dissipation dilution of the two coupled modes. In the short-coupler limit, $k_cl_c\ll1$, the symmetric-mode coupler undergoes nearly uniform rotation, and its torsional strain energy vanishes asymptotically. The remaining loss contributions arise from polygon-side bending and supporting-tether torsion. The reduced supporting-tether contribution allows the symmetric-mode dissipation dilution to exceed that of an isolated polygon with the same side and supporting-tether dimensions. The antisymmetric mode retains torsional strain in the coupler and has an additional loss contribution. We also derive an expression for $Q\cdot f$ in the short-coupler and short-tether limits, where $Q$ is the mechanical quality factor and $f$ is the resonance frequency. This expression gives the dependence of $Q\cdot f$ on tensile stress, film thickness, and supporting-tether geometry. For a coupler length of $100~μ\mathrm{m}$ and width of $2~μ\mathrm{m}$, finite element calculations give a frequency splitting of $17.7~\mathrm{Hz}$ and a symmetric-mode dilution factor approximately $13\%$ above the analytical isolated-polygon value.

infographic.key_insight: Tuning the shared tether between two square resonators controls frequency splitting and can enhance symmetric-mode dissipation dilution beyond that of an isolated polygon.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coupler geometry offers a design lever for coupled mechanical resonators with tunable mode separation and reduced dissipation.
method: Develop a continuum model linking coupler length and width to mode splitting and dissipation dilution.
Compare analytical predictions with finite element simulations.
Derive short-coupler mode behavior and a short-coupler, short-tether expression for Q·f.
infographic.evidence_signal: For a 100 μm-long, 2 μm-wide coupler, finite element calculations yield 17.7 Hz frequency splitting and symmetric-mode dilution approximately 13% above the analytical isolated-polygon value.
infographic.watch_item: The simplified loss and Q·f expressions rely on short-coupler or short-tether limits, and the abstract reports simulation comparisons rather than experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Coupled Soft-Clamped Polygon Resonators with Tunable Mechanical Coupling

title: Allen--Cahn Residual-Constrained Topology Optimization via an Augmented Lagrangian Method
authors: Run Du, Xuan Xiao, Wenming Cheng, Zeqiang Zhang
abstract: This paper presents a residual-constrained topology optimization framework that controls interface transition bandwidth without requiring external density filters. The steady conserved Allen--Cahn (AC) equation is formulated as an equality residual constraint and solved via a mass-weighted Augmented Lagrangian Method (ALM) coupled with the Method of Moving Asymptotes (MMA). A closed-form chemical potential projection eliminates the constant residual mode, ensuring algebraic compatibility with external volume targets. Variational sensitivity analysis reveals a symmetric-plus-rank-one Jacobian that yields matrix-free sensitivities without additional adjoint PDE solves, reducing residual sensitivity overhead to only 0.11% of the state elasticity solve time in 3D. Systematic 2D benchmarks confirm that interface bandwidth is governed intrinsically by reaction--diffusion parameters across mesh refinements. While diffuse interfaces incur a continuous compliance elevation (1.4%--12.3%), a volume-preserving 0/1 post-processing audit across 48 benchmark cases demonstrates that this gap stems primarily from intermediate-density penalization: binarized AC-ALM designs achieve equal or superior stiffness in 45 configurations (averaging 1.2% stiffer than SIMP). Simultaneously, single-node hinges and strut fragmentation are substantially suppressed compared to unregularized baselines. Three-dimensional benchmarks further demonstrate practical spatial viability for complex structures.

infographic.key_insight: Constraining the conserved Allen–Cahn residual controls topology interface bandwidth intrinsically, without external density filters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework suppresses single-node hinges and strut fragmentation while supporting complex 3D structural topology optimization.
method: Enforce the steady conserved Allen–Cahn residual using a mass-weighted augmented Lagrangian method coupled with MMA.
Project the chemical potential to remove the constant residual mode and maintain compatibility with prescribed volume targets.
Exploit a symmetric-plus-rank-one Jacobian for matrix-free residual sensitivities without additional adjoint PDE solves.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 48 benchmark cases, volume-preserving binarized designs matched or exceeded SIMP stiffness in 45 cases and averaged 1.2% stiffer; 3D residual sensitivity overhead was 0.11% of the elasticity solve time.
infographic.watch_item: Diffuse designs showed 1.4%–12.3% higher compliance; the reported stiffness advantage applies to volume-preserving binarized designs.
infographic.paper_title: Allen--Cahn Residual-Constrained Topology Optimization via an Augmented Lagrangian Method

title: Three-dimensional computational rheometry of viscoplastic fluids in vane-in-cup fixtures
authors: James Malcolm, Clare McColgan, Emma Mullarkey, Emad Chaparian
abstract: We develop a computational framework to investigate the flow kinematics of viscoplastic materials, described by the Herschel-Bulkley model, in vane-in-cup rheometers. Numerical simulations are performed using augmented Lagrangian finite element and regularised finite volume methods for two- and three-dimensional configurations, respectively, to characterise the hydrodynamics and yielding behaviour over a broad range of effective parameters. Three types of vanes are investigated: conventional 4- and 6-arm bespoke vanes and a 24-arm fractal vane (Owens et al., J. Rheol., vol. 64(3), 2020, 643-662). Our previous two-dimensional study (Chaparian et al., J. Non-Newtonian Fluid Mech., vol. 307, 2022, 104857) demonstrated the superiority of the fractal vane over conventional N-arm designs. The bespoke vanes produce highly non-uniform yielding, leading to significant deviations from the circular Couette analogy, whereas the 24-arm fractal vane generates nearly axisymmetric yield surfaces that effectively "cloak" the vane geometry. Consequently, the resulting flow closely resembles the azimuthal shear in a conventional "bob & cup" rheometer, providing substantially more accurate rheological measurements. Building on these findings, the present study revisits the torque-to-stress and rotation-to-strain rate conversions used in vane-in-cup rheometry. In particular, we re-examine the circular Couette analogy that underpins both the physical interpretation of the flow and the extraction of flow curves from raw rheometric data. Based on our extensive two- and three-dimensional simulations, we identify limitations of the existing conversion relations and propose improved closure expressions that enable more accurate determination of material's rheological properties. Furthermore, the three-dimensional flow structures and yielding patterns within the vane-in-cup fixtures are characterised.

infographic.key_insight: Simulations support improved vane-rheometry conversion relations, with the 24-arm fractal vane producing nearly axisymmetric yielding that better approximates circular Couette flow.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Better torque-to-stress and rotation-to-strain-rate conversions can improve rheological property measurements for viscoplastic materials.
method: Model Herschel–Bulkley fluids in vane-in-cup fixtures.
Use augmented Lagrangian finite elements in 2D and regularised finite volumes in 3D.
Compare 4-arm, 6-arm and 24-arm fractal vanes to refine conversion closures.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive 2D and 3D simulations across effective parameters, examining flow kinematics, yielding patterns and limitations of existing conversion relations.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental validation and quantitative error reductions for the proposed closures are not reported in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Three-dimensional computational rheometry of viscoplastic fluids in vane-in-cup fixtures

title: High-Order Unconditionally Stable IMEX BDF--FEM Schemes for the Hodgkin--Huxley Model on a Branched Axon
authors: Hayden Reed, Qingguang Guan
abstract: We construct and analyze high-order implicit--explicit backward differentiation formula finite element (IMEX BDF--FEM) schemes for the Hodgkin--Huxley cable system on a branched metric graph. The linearly implicit schemes combine constant-step BDF methods of orders $q=1,\ldots,5$ with conforming finite elements of any fixed degree $p\ge1$. Extrapolated gate variables are smoothly masked before evaluating the conductances, preserving coercivity without projecting the numerical gates. A voltage cutoff makes the gate rates globally bounded and Lipschitz. Each timestep requires one linear voltage solve followed by independent nodal gate updates. Under exact spatial integration, we prove unconditional stability of the complete fully discrete regularized scheme in discrete history energies. Under regularity and starting-history assumptions, the voltage and reconstructed gates converge in $L^2(Γ)$ at the optimal rate $O(h^{p+1}+Δt^q)$, without a timestep restriction or an $h$--$Δt$ coupling. The same rate holds with numerical quadrature when its full residual defect is $O(h^{p+1})$. Manufactured solutions recover the predicted orders through BDF5--$P_4$. Action-potential simulations illustrate pulse propagation and splitting, while a controlled work--precision comparison within the proposed family shows that higher-order variants can reach a prescribed accuracy at much lower runtime along the tested joint-refinement paths.

infographic.key_insight: High-order IMEX BDF–FEM schemes achieve unconditional stability and optimal convergence for a regularized Hodgkin–Huxley model on branched axons without coupling timestep size to mesh spacing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports accurate, efficient simulation of electrical pulse propagation and splitting in branched neural cables.
method: Combine BDF orders 1–5 with conforming finite elements of any fixed degree p ≥ 1.
Smoothly mask extrapolated gates and cut off voltage-dependent rates to enable stability analysis.
Use one linear voltage solve per timestep, followed by independent nodal gate updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Manufactured solutions recover predicted orders through BDF5–P4, while action-potential simulations and within-family work–precision tests demonstrate propagation, splitting, and lower runtime for higher-order variants along tested refinement paths.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees apply to the regularized model under stated assumptions; numerical quadrature must keep its full residual defect at O(h^{p+1}) to preserve optimal convergence.
infographic.paper_title: High-Order Unconditionally Stable IMEX BDF--FEM Schemes for the Hodgkin--Huxley Model on a Branched Axon

title: A Legendre-Based Modified Extreme Learning Machine for Convection-Diffusion Equations: Steady-State, Continuous-Time, and Discrete-Time Formulations
authors: Gadade Navnath Ankush, Ram Shiromani, Tomas Gandara, Ramon Codina, Sivaram Ambikasaran
abstract: Convection-diffusion equations are fundamental models for transport phenomena, but their numerical solution becomes challenging in convection-dominated regimes due to steep gradients and sharp boundary layers. This motivates the development of accurate approaches capable of effectively resolving such features while avoiding costly iterative optimization. In this study, a modified ELM framework based on shifted Legendre polynomials is developed for convection-diffusion equations in steady-state, continuous-time, and discrete-time formulations. The proposed approach is evaluated on steady and unsteady benchmark problems with relatively high Peclet numbers, including continuous and discontinuous boundary conditions. Finite element method solutions are used as independent solution references. By exploiting the linearity of the governing equations, MELM determines the output weights through a single least-squares solve, avoiding the iterative gradient-based training required by PINNs. The shifted Legendre polynomial basis provides an effective spectral representation for resolving steep gradients and sharp boundary layers. For the DT-MELM formulation, the coefficient matrix remains unchanged across successive time levels, allowing its LU or QR factorization to be computed once and reused. A systematic comparison with PINNs that incorporate advanced training strategies demonstrates that MELM provides higher accuracy and shorter solution times for steady-state and DT-MELM formulations across the benchmark problems considered. In contrast, CT-MELM exhibits scalability limitations as the size of the space--time basis increases. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of MELM for steady-state and discrete-time convection--diffusion problems, while also showing that PINNs provide better scalability for large space--time formulations where global CT-MELM becomes computationally demanding.

infographic.key_insight: Legendre-based modified extreme learning machines solve linear convection–diffusion problems without iterative training, outperforming tested PINNs in accuracy and solution time for steady-state and discrete-time formulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers an efficient option for transport simulations with steep gradients and sharp boundary layers in convection-dominated regimes.
method: Represent solutions using shifted Legendre polynomial bases.
Determine output weights through a single least-squares solve using the linear governing equations.
Reuse the coefficient-matrix LU or QR factorization across discrete time steps.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covers steady and unsteady high-Peclet benchmarks with continuous and discontinuous boundary conditions, using FEM references and comparisons against PINNs with advanced training strategies.
infographic.watch_item: Global continuous-time MELM becomes computationally demanding as the space–time basis grows; PINNs showed better scalability for large space–time formulations.
infographic.paper_title: A Legendre-Based Modified Extreme Learning Machine for Convection-Diffusion Equations: Steady-State, Continuous-Time, and Discrete-Time Formulations

title: Thermodynamic Underpinnings Affecting Compressive and Tensile Plasticity in Refractory Compositionally Complex Alloys
authors: Eric A. Lass, Carla Joyce C. Nocheseda, Christopher Tandoc, Yong-Jie Hu, Peter K. Liaw
abstract: Refractory compositionally complex alloys (R-CCAs) show great promise as next generation structural materials for extreme conditions, but alloys with excellent high temperature mechanical properties most often exhibit virtually zero room temperature tensile ductility, hindering potential commercial application. Several semi-empirical metrics have been employed for predicting plasticity in R-CCAs, including valence electron concentration, Pugh ratio, Rice criteria, and the D-parameter. While many currently available ductility metrics correlate very well when compressive plasticity is considered, only the density functional theory (DFT) based D-parameter shows a strong correlation in tension. A new ductility metric is developed using CALculation of PHAse Diagrams (CALPHAD) thermodynamics, Gamma, with includes the free energy difference between the body-centered cubic (BCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phases, the interfacial free energy of a (110) BCC surface, and an electronegativity-corrected lattice distortion. The Gamma parameter exhibits better correlation with tensile ductility than D-parameter and performs equally well in compression. While this improvement is modest, a thermodynamically grounded ductility metric is clearly required to capture intrinsic ductility behavior. Extrinsic contributions to brittle behavior in R-CCAs, namely interstitial oxygen content, are also briefly discussed. Combining the Gamma ductility parameter with CALPHAD-calculated oxygen solubility is proposed as a first order attempt to capture both intrinsic and extrinsic contributions to ductile behavior in R-CCAs.

infographic.key_insight: The CALPHAD-based Γ ductility metric modestly improves correlation with tensile ductility in refractory compositionally complex alloys while matching the DFT-based D-parameter in compression.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Γ could guide screening of refractory alloys for room-temperature ductility, a key barrier to deploying these materials in extreme-condition structures.
method: Combine the BCC–HCP free-energy difference with the interfacial free energy of a (110) BCC surface.
Include electronegativity-corrected lattice distortion in the Γ metric.
Compare ductility correlations and propose pairing Γ with CALPHAD-calculated oxygen solubility.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports better tensile-ductility correlation than the D-parameter and equally good performance in compression, but provides no dataset size or quantitative correlation statistics.
infographic.watch_item: Γ targets intrinsic ductility; combining it with oxygen solubility to capture extrinsic embrittlement remains a proposed first-order approach.
infographic.paper_title: Thermodynamic Underpinnings Affecting Compressive and Tensile Plasticity in Refractory Compositionally Complex Alloys

title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI
authors: Oswaldo Ludwig
abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.

infographic.key_insight: DRAP reduces catastrophic forgetting by limiting updates to model tensors that supported prior actions at dynamically sensitive points in robot trajectories.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For sequential robot-skill adaptation, preserving behavior near amplification-prone states can help prevent small action errors from cascading into closed-loop failures.
method: Fit ridge-regularized local dynamics to expert transitions and estimate perturbation amplification using the largest singular value of the state-transition matrix.
Accumulate risk-weighted squared action gradients into a replay-free, tensor-level importance memory.
Use normalized cumulative importance to scale each tensor’s effective AdamW learning rate.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a fixed KappaTune-selected OpenVLA subnetwork adapted sequentially across LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites, the abstract reports better retention than AdamW and EWC while maintaining strong new-suite acquisition.
infographic.watch_item: The local, one-step amplification estimate is not a guarantee of long-horizon stability, and evidence is limited to the reported robot-learning setup rather than constitutive modeling.
infographic.paper_title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI

title: TB-Transolver: Parallelized and Coherent Long-Horizon Rollouts via Temporal Bundling for Time-Dependent PDEs
authors: Sidharth S. Menon, Ameya D. Jagtap
abstract: Transolver has recently gained widespread adoption for solving diverse physical problems on unstructured geometric meshes by leveraging its Physics-Attention mechanism, which seamlessly extends standard softmax attention to handle physical domains at scale. For time-dependent problems, existing literature relies on time-conditioned or autoregressive rollouts to preserve temporal causality while retaining Physics-Attention as the spatial backbone. However, a fundamental limitation of this formulation is its sequential execution model, wherein computational costs scale linearly with the temporal horizon, rendering standard Transolver inefficient for transient problems despite its exceptional spatial efficacy. This bottleneck has historically hindered its broader application in time-dependent physical modeling. To address this limitation, we introduce TB-Transolver (also referred to as Temporally Bundled Transolver), an efficient framework built on temporal bundling that scales Transolver for time-dependent PDEs. Furthermore, we propose \emph{spatiotemporal coherence} (${\rm C(K)}$) as a general metric to systematically quantify snapshot correlation within a temporal bundle, enabling the \emph{a priori} selection of optimal bundle widths using training data alone, thereby avoiding expensive grid searches. We demonstrate the computational efficacy of TB-Transolver across four physically distinct domains, namely, plasticity, fluid dynamics, reaction-diffusion, and global weather forecasting; achieving training speedups of up to $29\times$ over conventional autoregressive and time-conditioned baselines. Finally, these computational gains are further amplified through distributed multi-node and multi-GPU parallelism, yielding aggregated speedups of up to $45.6\times$ at optimal bundle widths for systems exhibiting high spatiotemporal coherence compared to single-GPU implementations.

infographic.key_insight: TB-Transolver uses temporal bundling to reduce sequential rollout costs for time-dependent PDEs while retaining Transolver’s Physics-Attention spatial backbone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could accelerate transient engineering simulations, including plasticity, where long time horizons make sequential prediction costly.
method: Bundle temporal snapshots to enable parallelized long-horizon prediction.
Use spatiotemporal coherence C(K) to select bundle widths from training data without expensive grid searches.
Combine temporal bundling with distributed multi-node, multi-GPU execution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across plasticity, fluid dynamics, reaction-diffusion, and global weather forecasting, the abstract reports training speedups up to 29× over autoregressive and time-conditioned baselines, and aggregated speedups up to 45.6× versus single-GPU implementations.
infographic.watch_item: The largest gains depend on high spatiotemporal coherence and optimal bundle widths; the abstract does not quantify long-horizon prediction accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: TB-Transolver: Parallelized and Coherent Long-Horizon Rollouts via Temporal Bundling for Time-Dependent PDEs

title: Fracture-Bench: A Controlled Benchmark Suite for Machine Learning Surrogates in Phase-Field Fracture Mechanics
authors: Meenu Krishnan U., Maryam Hakimzadeh, Indrashish Saha, Meer Mehran Rashid, Lori Graham-Brady, Somdatta Goswami
abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly proposed to replace phase-field fracture simulations in many-query tasks such as uncertainty quantification, inverse analysis and design. Little controlled evidence shows which architectures are reliable, for which fracture problems and how far beyond their training data. We introduce Fracture-Bench, an open benchmark of two phase-field datasets with fixed splits, common test metrics and a description of each dataset's physical regime. Dataset~1 contains 1,000 AT2 simulations of multiple cracks growing from a notched hole in a hyperelastic plate under random non-uniform biaxial boundary displacements (44 load steps, $128\times128$ grid). Dataset~2 contains 4,000 PF-CZM simulations of a pre-cracked plate with two inclusions, each ten times stiffer or more compliant than the matrix ($128\times256$ grid). We train a Fourier neural operator (FNO), DeepONet, Latent DeepONet, a UNet and a conditional diffusion model on identical splits and compare one test metric per dataset, training time, inference time and model size. On Dataset~1, FNO and Latent DeepONet attain mean test errors of order $10^{-6}$, about ten times lower than UNet and DeepONet. On Dataset~2, the diffusion model is most accurate, with about one sixth of the UNet error, but requires \SI{706}{s} per prediction versus \SI{6}{ms} for UNet. For all architectures, most of the error occurs in the final load steps, after crack localization. Dataset~2 contains initial cracks less than one grid cell apart that produce qualitatively different paths. Architecture rankings therefore depend on the task, and errors averaged over densely sampled inputs reveal little about near-bifurcation cases. Data, codes, splits, regime descriptors and generalization splits are public, with a protocol for adding under-represented regimes such as mixed-mode, three-dimensional and experimentally paired fracture.

infographic.key_insight: The best fracture surrogate depends on the task: FNO and Latent DeepONet lead on Dataset 1, while diffusion is most accurate but far slower on Dataset 2.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fracture-Bench supports task-specific surrogate selection for uncertainty quantification, inverse analysis and design by comparing accuracy, speed and model size.
method: Benchmark 1,000 AT2 simulations of a notched hyperelastic plate and 4,000 PF-CZM simulations of a pre-cracked plate with stiffness-contrast inclusions.
Train FNO, DeepONet, Latent DeepONet, UNet and conditional diffusion models on identical splits.
Evaluate dataset-specific test error, training time, inference time and model size.
infographic.evidence_signal: FNO and Latent DeepONet achieve mean test errors of order 10⁻⁶ on Dataset 1; on Dataset 2, diffusion has about one-sixth of UNet's error but takes 706 s per prediction versus 6 ms.
infographic.watch_item: Average errors can obscure near-bifurcation failures: Dataset 2 includes initial cracks less than one grid cell apart that produce qualitatively different paths.
infographic.paper_title: Fracture-Bench: A Controlled Benchmark Suite for Machine Learning Surrogates in Phase-Field Fracture Mechanics

title: Structured Neural Network Models for Anisotropic Magnetic Constitutive Laws
authors: Dorian Zeilinger, Felix Engertsberger, Herbert Egger
abstract: High-performance electrical steel used for iron cores of power transformers and generators exhibits complex material behavior. While modeling and simulation of isotropic nonlinear response is well understood, the incorporation of magnetic anisotropy remains challenging. This work proposes to utilize a structured neural network architecture to systematically describe the anisotropic nonlinear anhysteretic magnetic material response of electrical steel sheets. By constructing a convex and smooth co-energy density with dedicated behavior at infinity, we can ensure thermodynamic consistency and correct physical behavior and further guarantee basic mathematical properties which provide well-posedness of corresponding magnetic field problems and efficient numerical solvers. Numerical tests demonstrate the capability of the proposed method to describe strongly anisotropic behavior as well as its robust convergence in finite-element simulations.

infographic.key_insight: A structured neural network models anisotropic, nonlinear magnetic response through a smooth, convex co-energy density with controlled behavior at infinity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports physically consistent magnetic-field simulations of electrical steel sheets used in transformer and generator cores.
method: Represent anhysteretic magnetic behavior using a structured neural network.
Enforce smoothness, convexity, and prescribed asymptotic behavior in the co-energy density.
Build in properties supporting well-posed magnetic-field problems and efficient numerical solvers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests demonstrate strongly anisotropic response modeling and robust convergence in finite-element simulations.
infographic.watch_item: The model targets anhysteretic response; hysteresis and associated magnetic losses are outside the stated scope.
infographic.paper_title: Structured Neural Network Models for Anisotropic Magnetic Constitutive Laws
